summary: A 1974 discussion and proposal for a common command language that users could use across different network services, called the Unified User-Level Protocol. The idea was to spare users from learning a different set of commands for every host. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: Every computer used to have its own commands. This note suggests one shared set of commands so people only learn them once.

subtitle: A common command language so users could work across different ARPANET servers with one set of commands

tldr.problem: Every ARPANET host had its own command language, forcing users to learn multiple command sets or remember which commands worked on which system.
tldr.mechanism: The Unified User-Level Protocol proposes a single set of generic commands for common operations like login, mail, file manipulation and program invocation that could be implemented by translating to each host's native commands.
tldr.outcome: Although the UULP itself was not widely adopted, the idea of a common command language influenced later terminal and remote access protocols, and was eventually succeeded by more sophisticated solutions.

facts.label: Case handling
facts.value: Commands case-insensitive; arguments may be case-sensitive

today: The UULP was not widely adopted as specified. However, its principles influenced later user interface protocols. The concept of a common command language eventually evolved into standardized interfaces through shell conventions and later, graphical and web-based interfaces. Today, SSH and modern login systems provide similar unified access across diverse hosts.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goal
sections.content:
By 1974, the ARPANET connected diverse computer systems, each with its own command languages and conventions. A user trying to work across multiple systems had to remember or look up different syntax for common tasks: login, file listing, mail, and file transfer. The Unified User-Level Protocol (UULP) proposes a solution: a single, shared command language that all network servers would understand, implemented as an option within Telnet.

The name "Unified User-Level Protocol" reflects the goal of creating unity across diverse systems while remaining at the user interaction level, leaving each host's internal command language unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers each used different words for the same jobs. A protocol was proposed so that one set of words would work everywhere.

sections.title: Core Commands
sections.content:
The UULP defines a set of commands for the most common needs. The login command lets a user authenticate with any server, accepting both local identifiers and network-wide names prefixed with an asterisk (like *free for a guest account). The help command provides documentation, with variants for system help, UULP-specific help, or help on individual commands.

For communication, the protocol supports mail (send and receive), readmail (check one's mailbox), who (find out who is logged in), and concom (console-to-console messaging). File operations include type (display file contents), copy, delete, rename, and listdir (list directory contents). The call command invokes programs, with special names like -pl1, -fortran and -basic for language processors. local exits the UULP environment to access native commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol defined commands for logging in, sending mail, listing files, and running programs. All the things people do most often.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The UULP is designed for "front-endability"—that is, servers could implement it by translating the common commands into their existing native command syntax, rather than replacing those native systems. This makes adoption easier and preserves the work already invested in each host's command system.

All UULP commands are case-insensitive (can be typed in upper or lower case), and arguments are specified in advance on the command line rather than requested interactively. This allows both human users and automated programs (such as shell scripts) to use the same command set. The protocol uses literal, plain-text responses (such as "Invalid ident: username") rather than numeric codes, to be readable to humans and to avoid the ambiguities that arise with code-based systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The design let each computer keep its own way of doing things underneath, while presenting the same buttons on top. That way, old commands could still work, but new ones would be shared.

sections.title: Implementation Context
sections.content:
The UULP is initially proposed as a negotiated option in the Telnet protocol, meaning a Telnet server could offer to switch into UULP mode if the client requests it. The protocol is meant to be a "selector" that can exit to other environments (the local command processor, FTP, RJE) via special commands, and eventually the UULP might become the default entry point for all network login.

Because of differences in how systems handle case sensitivity, the UULP includes optional support for a map command to help users on systems with case-sensitive filenames who are logging in from uppercase-only terminals. Line ending characters can be customized with eol, and erase and kill characters can be set with erase and kill. A prompt command lets users specify a known prompt character so that programs can reliably detect when the server is ready for the next command.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea was to add this on top of Telnet, so when you logged in, you would see a friendly set of commands instead of learning each computer's own way.
